files.lesson.md: --- order: 12 unit: fractions node: AC9M7N06 n1 assumes: [AC9M5N05 n1] uses: [AC9M7N04 n1, AC9M7N02 n3] # equivalent fractions; the LCM (HCF and LCM) title: Adding and subtracting fractions summary: "Parts can be counted together only when they are the same size. Cut both fractions into the same parts first: 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12. The lowest common multiple of the bottoms is the smallest choice." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } connection: timber-cuts # data/connections/maths.yml hook: "A recipe needs 1/2 of a cup of milk and 1/5 of a cup of cream. How much is that altogether? You cannot tell until the parts are the same size." app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8269 url: http://127.0.0.1:8269/index.html readySelector: "#sl-k" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: bars.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Cut into twelfths, $\\tfrac{1}{3} = \\tfrac{4}{12}$ and $\\tfrac{1}{4} = \\tfrac{3}{12}$: together 7 twelfths." } explainClip: query: { code: "@bars.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "The same size parts" say: "Thirds and quarters cannot be counted together." clip: - caption: { text: "9 parts: thirds split, quarters do not.", say: "Nine parts: the quarters do not split evenly." } - wait: 1200 - caption: { text: "12 parts: both split. 12 is the LCM of 3 and 4.", say: "Twelve parts: both split. Twelve is the lowest common multiple." } - click: Make k bigger - click: Make k bigger - click: Make k bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12" } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "4 twelfths + 3 twelfths = 7 twelfths.", say: "Four twelfths and three twelfths make seven twelfths." } - wait: 1400 --- You can add 2 apples and 3 apples, but 2 apples and 3 pears do not make 5 of anything. Fractions are the same: $\tfrac{2}{7} + \tfrac{3}{7} = \tfrac{5}{7}$ (sevenths and sevenths), but thirds and quarters are different sizes. To add or subtract fractions with different bottoms, cut both into the **same parts** first, using equivalent fractions. The new bottom is a **common denominator**: a common multiple of the two bottoms, and the lowest common multiple is the smallest. ## Predict: a third and a quarter ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a sum for 1/3 + 1/4 shows whether they add the tops and the bottoms (2/7), which the bars then contradict." check: type: predict q: "What is $\\tfrac{1}{3} + \\tfrac{1}{4}$?" options: ["$\\tfrac{7}{12}$", "$\\tfrac{2}{7}$", "$\\tfrac{2}{12}$", "$\\tfrac{1}{7}$"] actual: "7/12: 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, and 4 + 3 = 7 twelfths. 2/7 is less than 1/3 on its own, so it cannot be the sum." ``` Is the answer more or less than $\tfrac{1}{3}$ on its own? ## Run: cut them the same ```step stage: run insight: "Changing the number of parts until both bars split evenly shows that a common multiple of 3 and 4 makes the parts countable." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Change $k$, the number of parts in each whole, until both fractions split evenly. Then read the sum. Was your prediction right?", when: "e = 1", explain: "12 works (and 24): both are multiples of 3 and 4. 12 is the lowest." } ``` The board says when a bar does not split evenly into $k$ parts. ## Investigate: common denominators ```step stage: investigate insight: "A common denominator makes the parts the same size; Ella adds tops and bottoms as if the parts already matched. Mixed numerals and decimals follow the same rule: line up like with like." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\tfrac{2}{5} + \\tfrac{1}{3}$. Give your answer in simplest form." answer: "11/15" form: simplest feedback: - ["3/8", "That adds the tops and the bottoms. Cut both into fifteenths first."] - ["3/15", "Change the tops too: 2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15."] explain: "2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15, so 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ella" text: "Ella adds $\\tfrac{1}{2} + \\tfrac{1}{3}$. Click the line where her method goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: fraction-add-across explain: "Line 2: halves and thirds are different sizes, so they cannot be counted together. 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6: 5/6. (2/5 is less than 1/2 on its own.)" - check: type: answer q: "Work out $3.45 + 2.7$." answer: "6.15" feedback: - ["3.72", "The 7 is 7 tenths, not 7 hundredths. Line up the decimal points: 2.70."] - ["6.42", "That lines up the last digits. Line up the decimal points instead: 2.7 = 2.70."] explain: "Line up the points: 3.45 + 2.70 = 6.15. Tenths with tenths, like fractions with the same bottom." ``` ### Same parts, then count Here is the method, then a mixed numeral and a decimal. ```worked \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{4}{12} + \tfrac{3}{12} :: The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12: write both in twelfths. = \tfrac{7}{12} :: Same parts: add the tops, keep the bottom. 2\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{10}{4} - \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{7}{4} = 1\tfrac{3}{4} :: A mixed numeral: write it as quarters first. 3.45 + 2.70 = 6.15 :: Decimals: line up the points (the same parts: tenths, hundredths). ``` Now try one: $\tfrac{2}{5} + \tfrac{1}{3}$. ### Find the mistake Read Ella's working. Could the answer be less than $\tfrac{1}{2}$? ### Decimals ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: subtracting on the board with the lowest common denominator, subtracting without the board, a mixed numeral answer, then the case where one denominator is a multiple of the other." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#subtract", height: 600 } tasks: - starter: "bars.yml#subtract" hint: "24 works. Is there a smaller number that 4 and 6 both divide?" check: { type: board, text: "Find $\\tfrac{3}{4} - \\tfrac{1}{6}$ with the lowest common denominator.", when: "e = 1 and l = 1", explain: "12: 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/6 = 2/12, so 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12." } - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\tfrac{5}{6} - \\tfrac{1}{4}$ in simplest form." answer: "7/12" form: simplest feedback: - ["4/2", "Subtracting the tops and the bottoms does not work for different parts."] - ["14/24", "Equal, but it simplifies: 12 is a smaller common denominator."] explain: "5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so 7/12." - check: type: answer q: "Work out $1\\tfrac{1}{2} + \\tfrac{2}{3}$." answer: "2 1/6" form: simplest feedback: - ["1 3/5", "Adding tops and bottoms does not work. Write both in sixths."] explain: "1 1/2 = 9/6 and 2/3 = 4/6, so 13/6 = 2 1/6." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: what is the lowest common denominator for $\\tfrac{1}{4} + \\tfrac{3}{8}$?" options: ["8, since 8 is already a multiple of 4", "32 = 4 × 8", "12 = 4 + 8", "4"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "32 works, but 8 is lower: 4 divides 8.", "12 is not a multiple of 8.", "Eighths do not split into quarters."] explain: "4 divides 8, so only the 1/4 changes: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8." ``` ### Subtract Each task changes one thing. ### Without the board ### A mixed numeral ### One already fits ## Practise: add and subtract ```step stage: practise insight: "Fractions, a mixed numeral and decimals in context, mixed; adding across is the planted slip; the review keeps the LCM fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\tfrac{3}{4} + \\tfrac{1}{6}$ in simplest form." answer: "11/12" form: simplest feedback: - ["4/10", "That adds the tops and the bottoms."] explain: "9/12 + 2/12 = 11/12." - check: type: answer q: "Work out $3\\tfrac{1}{3} - 1\\tfrac{1}{2}$." answer: "1 5/6" form: simplest feedback: - ["2", "The wholes give 2, but 1/3 − 1/2 is less than zero. Write both as sixths: 20/6 − 9/6."] explain: "3 1/3 = 20/6 and 1 1/2 = 9/6, so 11/6 = 1 5/6." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "How many sixths are there in $3\\tfrac{1}{3}$?", answer: 20, explain: "3 wholes are 18 sixths and a third is 2 sixths: 20 sixths. Now do the same for $1\\tfrac{1}{2}$." } - check: type: answer q: "A plank is 2.4 m long. 0.65 m is cut off. How long is the rest, in metres?" answer: "1.75" feedback: - ["2.35", "The 65 is hundredths. Line up the points: 2.40 − 0.65."] explain: "2.40 − 0.65 = 1.75 m." - check: type: answer q: "Review: find the LCM of 6 and 10." answer: "30" feedback: - ["60", "6 × 10 counts the shared 2 twice."] explain: "6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5: LCM = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30." ``` ### Add ### Mixed numerals ### Decimals in context ### Review: LCM ## Make: a sum of one ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing two different fractions that add to exactly 1, and showing it with a common denominator, works the method backwards." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#make", height: 680 } hint: ["Try 1/2 and something else, or 1/3 and something else.", "Choose k so both bars split, then count the parts."] check: { type: board, text: "Make two fractions with different bottoms that add to exactly 1.", when: "o = 1 and r = 1 and (b - d)^2 > 0 and e = 1 and a > 0 and c > 0 and a < b and c < d", explain: "For example 1/2 + 2/4, 1/3 + 4/6 or 1/4 + 6/8. Neither bottom a multiple of the other: 2/4 + 3/6 (6/12 + 6/12)." } ``` Then find a pair where neither bottom is a multiple of the other. ## Make: a board on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Lining up the places before taking away is the move that fails when students subtract 85 from 24; the paper task makes them set it out and choose why." hint: ["Write 2.4 as 2.40 so the places line up.", "Take away both pieces: add them first, or subtract one at a time."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A shelf kit needs two pieces cut from one 2.4 m board: one 0.85 m long and one 1.25 m long. How much of the board is left, in metres?" steps: - ["Write the lengths with the same places: $2.40$, $0.85$, $1.25$", "tenths with tenths and hundredths with hundredths, like fractions with the same bottom"] - ["$0.85 + 1.25 = 2.10$", "the two pieces together"] - ["$2.40 - 2.10 = 0.30$", "take the pieces away from the board"] - ["$0.3$ m is left", "check: 2.10 + 0.30 = 2.40, the whole board"] picks: - step: 1 q: "Why write 2.4 as 2.40 before you take anything away?" options: - "So the places line up: hundredths sit under hundredths" - "So the answer has two decimal places" - "Because 2.4 is a different number from 2.40" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The places are the reason. The answer's length does not matter.", "They are the same number. Only the places are written differently."] answer: "0.3" feedback: - ["1.55", "That takes away only the 0.85 piece. The 1.25 piece comes off the board too."] criteria: - "I wrote every length to hundredths so the points lined up." - "I took away both pieces, not just one." - "I checked: the pieces and the offcut add back to 2.4 m." explain: "0.85 + 1.25 = 2.10, and 2.40 − 2.10 = 0.30. About 0.3 m (30 cm) is left. The saw takes a few millimetres from each cut, so in a real shed the offcut is a little shorter." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The lengths are made up for the task, but the question is real: someone cutting shelves has to know whether the board is long enough. Write the lengths with the points lined up, take both pieces away, and type the length left. **Also used in** - **Building.** Decking, skirting boards and fence rails are cut from stock lengths, and the offcut tells you whether one more piece fits. - **Cooking.** Recipes add and take away fractions of a cup, and the pieces have to be the same size first. - **Money.** Receipts and bank balances add and subtract in dollars and cents, tenths and hundredths. ```teacher summary: Students cut two fraction bars into the same number of parts to add and subtract fractions with different denominators, use the LCM as the lowest common denominator, and extend the idea to mixed numerals and decimals (AC9M7N06, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators using a common denominator. - I can add and subtract mixed numerals and decimals. - I can explain why the tops and the bottoms are not simply added. struggle: Finding a common denominator without guessing. Ask students to list a few multiples of each bottom number and look for the first match, instead of telling them the LCM. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need equivalent fractions (Equivalent fractions) and the LCM (HCF and LCM). The one idea: parts can be counted together only when they are the same size, so cut both fractions into the same parts first. The common mistake is adding the tops and the bottoms (Ella's mistake); a quick check is that the sum must be bigger than each fraction. Decimals are the same idea: line up the places so tenths are added to tenths. running: - "Predict: students who chose 2/7 added across. Ask: is 2/7 bigger than 1/3?" - "Run: ask which values of k work, and what they have in common." - "Investigate: for the decimals task, write 2.7 as 2.70 and ask why that is allowed." - "Modify: for the edge case, ask why only one fraction needs to change." - "Make: collect pairs; then challenge for one where neither bottom divides the other." - "Paper: the board task is worked in books; the page marks the answer (0.3) and the reason for writing 2.40. Books out, then look for the points lined up, not the answer alone." stuck: - see: A student adds the tops and the bottoms (Ella's mistake). ask: Is your answer bigger than each fraction you added? fix: "Use the bars: change both into the same parts, then count." - see: A student changes the bottom but not the top (1/3 = 1/12). ask: What did you multiply the bottom by? Did the top get the same? fix: "Equivalent fractions: the same multiplication on the top and the bottom." - see: A student subtracting mixed numerals takes the wholes and the parts separately and gets stuck at 1/3 − 1/2. ask: What if you write both as improper fractions first? fix: Convert to improper fractions with a common denominator, then subtract. stretch: Find three different fractions with different bottoms that add to 1. support: Use the board for every sum; fraction walls and a list of multiples help find the common denominator. leads: > Next: Multiplying and dividing fractions (node 2), where the rule is different: no common denominator needed. Where it leads: algebraic fractions (Year 10) and probability with fractions. exit: q: Work out 2/3 + 1/5 and 1 1/4 − 2/3. a: 10/15 + 3/15 = 13/15. 15/12 − 8/12 = 7/12. explain: > Fractions can be added only when the parts are the same size. Cut both into the same parts with equivalent fractions, using a **common denominator** (the LCM of the bottoms is the lowest): $\tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{4}{12} + \tfrac{3}{12} = \tfrac{7}{12}$. Then add the tops and keep the bottom. (Adding across gives $\tfrac{2}{7}$, which is less than $\tfrac{1}{3}$ alone.) For mixed numerals, change them to improper fractions first. For decimals, line up the points so tenths go with tenths. ```
